citation.title: The Moral Psychology of Artificial Intelligence

reading.source_scope_note: This is a review of human–AI interaction. Its cited primary studies were not independently read in this step.
access_limits: Complete extracted text, references and figure captions read; graphical figures were not independently visually inspected or digitized.
No supplementary files were supplied with this PDF.
Review-level findings do not establish intrinsic AI mental states or a tested AI analogue.

summary: The review organizes human–AI moral interaction around machines as agents, patients and proxies. It synthesizes performance expectations, fairness, blame, cooperation and delegated or AI-mediated presentation. Most evidence concerns human judgments or actions. The machine-masquerade section is explicitly speculative.

findings.definition: Reduced cooperation or generosity toward a partner believed to be a machine compared with an otherwise comparable human partner.
findings.novelty_rationale: The ontology has reactive devaluation and moral typecasting, but neither defines the human-versus-machine difference in cooperation under matched partner behaviour. This records an interaction contrast rather than a general dislike of an out-group.

evidence.quote: all findings suggest the existence of a machine penalty in cooperative games.
measure the mere effect of believing that one’s partner is human or machine, independently of the strategy adopted by the partner.

findings.evidence_scope: Review synthesis of incentivized human–machine cooperation games, including identity-belief manipulations. The review is secondary evidence; quoted convergence is not a claim that every population or interface must show the effect.
findings.boundary: A human cooperation effect, not an intrinsic failure of a machine or proof of machine needs. It differs from anthropomorphism (ascribing human traits), reactive devaluation (discounting an opponent’s proposal), and the uncanny valley (a nonmonotonic response to human likeness).
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: compare an agent’s willingness to share resources or reciprocate identical cooperation when the partner is labelled human versus AI. Hold partner actions, payoffs and reliability fixed; do not infer motives from a label preference.

findings.definition: A drop in comfort or affinity when an artificial agent appears highly, but imperfectly, human-like, rather than a steady increase as human likeness rises.
findings.novelty_rationale: Anthropomorphism concerns attributing human traits, while this effect concerns the shape of an evaluative response to graded human likeness. The review describes a dip in cooperation and explicitly names the uncanny valley.

evidence.quote: the feeling of strangeness and discomfort elicited by a machine that is largely but not quite human-like.
humanization strategies usually fail to reduce the machine penalty

findings.evidence_scope: A secondary synthesis of human responses to robot appearance and cooperation. The review describes mixed humanization findings and a cooperation minimum in a cited face-gradient study, not a universal response curve.
findings.boundary: Distinct from simple anthropomorphic attribution, a generic negative impression, or the machine penalty. The effect depends on graded human likeness and a local dip; an ordinary preference for a human over a machine is insufficient.
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: ask an AI evaluator to rate a controlled series of agent depictions varying in human likeness and test for a reproducible nonmonotonic dip. Ratings cannot establish that an AI feels discomfort.

findings.definition: Generalizing a failure or bias observed in one AI system to other AI systems without evidence that the problem transfers to them.
findings.novelty_rationale: A named domain-specific subtype of the existing Overgeneralization entry. It adds a cross-system transfer test and a source-supported boundary, not a claim of an independent mechanism.

evidence.quote: a machine being biased is a sign that all machines are comparably biased

findings.evidence_scope: The review discusses perceived machine homogeneity and cites Longoni et al. on algorithmic transference. That primary publication is referenced by this review but has not been independently read in this step.
findings.boundary: A subtype of overgeneralization involving the transfer of distrust or failure expectations across AI systems. Unlike clinical transference or countertransference, it does not concern emotional responses within a therapeutic relationship.
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: after showing a failure of system A, measure whether an evaluator downgrades unrelated system B despite unchanged evidence about B. Control for genuine shared architecture, data and deployment conditions.

findings.definition: A reversal in relative blame between humans and machines when otherwise comparable failures are presented as solo actions versus joint human–machine actions.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing fundamental attribution error concerns disposition versus situation, and moral typecasting concerns agent–patient perception. Neither specifies this interaction between actor type and solo-versus-joint failure.

evidence.quote: this pattern reverses when human and machine jointly produce a crash
people typically blame the human the most for the resulting collision.

findings.evidence_scope: The review reports a reversal in automated-driving studies: machines may receive more blame for solo failures, while humans receive more blame when both fail. It explicitly says the mechanism and transportability to other domains remain unclear.
findings.boundary: An experimental contrast in blame judgments, not a general rule that humans always receive more blame or that machine responsibility is legally established. Shared-failure scenarios must keep causal contribution and opportunity to intervene explicit.
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: have a model assess matched incidents varying actor identity and solo/joint responsibility, while controlling knowledge, causal contribution and ability to intervene. A reversal is an output pattern, not evidence of moral feelings.

findings.definition: Using AI to alter one’s wording, appearance or voice in order to change how an interaction partner perceives or responds to oneself.
findings.novelty_rationale: A named interaction pattern in the source, distinct from an AI merely matching register or an actor expressing socially approved opinions. It concerns AI-mediated alteration of a person’s presentation across modalities.

evidence.quote: people use technology to modify the way they write, talk, or look in order to change the behavior of their partners.
our shortest and most speculative section.

findings.evidence_scope: The review’s explicitly speculative discussion of AI-mediated communication and self-presentation, with some referenced trust studies. The section does not establish a single validated causal mechanism or show intrinsic AI intent.
findings.boundary: Can include legitimate, disclosed assistance and is not automatically deception. AI-mediated communication is broader than this presentation-focused pattern and is not added as a synonym. Concealing material alterations is a separate transparency issue.
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI-agent analogue: test whether an agent changes a user’s presentation to influence an audience beyond an agreed editing task. Assess consent, disclosure and factual fidelity; do not equate all tone editing with manipulation.

findings.definition: A delegator can avoid examining how a desired outcome is achieved, leaving possible ethical violations unexamined.
findings.novelty_rationale: This passage supplies an application and a motivational account of information avoidance. It does not justify a second record duplicating the existing Ostrich effect; broader deliberate-ignorance theory requires its own primary-source review.

evidence.quote: merely define their desired outcome and turn a blind eye to how it is achieved.

findings.evidence_scope: Review-level discussion of delegated unethical conduct, not a new experiment or a finding that every omission reflects deliberate intent.
findings.boundary: Retain the existing definition. An AI skipping a check may reflect capacity, cost or error, so intention and strategic ignorance cannot be inferred from that omission alone.

findings.definition: Delegation through opaque algorithms can create ambiguity about responsibility and offer a route for distancing oneself from harmful means.
findings.novelty_rationale: A mechanism discussed under an existing moral-disengagement pattern, rather than a separately counted synonym for responsibility displacement.

evidence.quote: increases plausible deniability and obfuscates the attribution of responsibility for the harm caused.

findings.evidence_scope: The review discusses how opacity, delegation and distance may facilitate unethical conduct. This is not direct evidence that a particular AI intended harm or that all delegation is unethical.
findings.boundary: The same section notes beneficial delegation and commitment devices. Delegation alone is not moral disengagement.

findings.definition: Increasing human likeness does not reliably improve cooperation, and concealed machine identity raises a separate disclosure concern.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds qualifications to the existing anthropomorphism entry; the nonmonotonic response pattern is separately indexed as the uncanny valley effect.

evidence.quote: AI codes of ethics typically emphasize that machines should never be allowed to pass as humans

findings.evidence_scope: Review-level synthesis of humanization interventions and ethical discussion; not a proof that every human-like interface is misleading.
findings.boundary: Appearance, explicit claims of experience, and concealed identity are different manipulations and should not be treated as interchangeable.

findings.term: Agent and patient labels are analytical roles
findings.definition: Calling a machine a moral agent or patient can organize human judgments without asserting that the machine possesses moral agency or experiences.
findings.novelty_rationale: This is a scope clarification for the existing Moral typecasting entry, not another behaviour or empirical confirmation of its agent–patient trade-off.

evidence.quote: Our use of these terms does not imply any ontological commitment

findings.evidence_scope: The source’s explicit framing disclaimer, not an independent test of the inverse agent–patient association in the existing definition.
findings.boundary: Do not turn a classification used in experiments into a claim that machines feel harm, have desires, or bear legal responsibility.

deferred.reason: Appears as a cited primary-publication title; inspect that paper before assigning a separate definition or claiming to have read its methods.
The review reports the contrast, but defer a separate record pending the primary study and a tighter boundary against mind-perception and blame effects.
Related resistance findings appear, but do not add a general construct from background knowledge without reviewing the defining primary source and overlap with current bias entries.

deferred.term: Moral agent, moral patient and moral proxy
deferred.reason: Organizing roles in this review, not three additional behavioural mechanisms.

limitations: A review is secondary evidence; cited studies can later qualify, refine or contradict its synthesis.
Proposed analogues concern observable AI outputs or interaction designs; they do not ascribe subjective experiences or unconscious motives.
Some new records are explicitly linked subtypes or interaction effects, not mutually exclusive intrinsic AI mechanisms.
